chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: Each lesson has a story or a picture, then small tools you use yourself. Lesson 9 revises the chapter with a quiz, a worksheet and a sample assessment. A closing look back ends the chapter.

points.title: Stories with a problem
points.text: Diksha, her father, Isha, Nitesh, Squiggly and Wiggly meet a real problem. A story names the idea, but it never gives away what you find out yourself.

points.title: You do it first
points.text: In the tools you build, fold, push, count and draw. Most tools show at once whether your try is right. The sample assessment shows its answers when you finish each section.

points.title: Questions from your maths book
points.text: Your maths book's questions sit inside the tool they belong to. Other tools have practice made for this chapter.

points.title: No timer, no score
points.text: Nothing is timed, scored or counted as a win. You get hints, you can try again and you can start over.

points.title: Clear, true pictures
points.text: A solid always looks like a solid. Each kind of solid keeps one colour. In sorting and matching games every solid is the same grey, so colour gives no clue.

points.title: Shapes in real life
points.text: Buildings, tents, wheels and spider webs show where shapes hide around us.

points.title: Revision and a look back
points.text: Lesson 9 has a recap story, a picture quiz, a worksheet and a sample assessment. Then a short look back shows earlier ideas again. Nothing new is taught there.

content.text: Diksha wanted to go to a big city during her summer holidays. Her father took her to Delhi and they visited many old and new interesting monuments like the India Gate, Qutub Minar, Safdarjung Tomb, Akshardham, the National Museum, Jantar Mantar and Sansad Bhawan. Now she is trying to make a model of India Gate using her wooden blocks.

tool_config.title: Shape Detective
tool_config.learning_objective: Students choose the block shape that models each part of a building and spot shapes hidden in a picture.
tool_config.screen: Frame, the same in every tool: progress dots on top; one stage on screen at a time; Back and Next at the sides and a Hint lamp that gives the four hints one at a time; a wrong try can be tried again and Reset starts the stage over; nothing is timed, scored or counted as a win. Stages that are not questions from your maths book carry a small tag, Practice. Your maths book's questions carry the book's own label, and after each try the screen shows the book's answer, which starts From the picture or Sample answer (open ones end Your answer may differ). First, Practice: one line says, Diksha wants a block for every part of a building. A floor mat holds light brown wooden blocks. There are a long flat block, a tall block and a cube. There are also a can-shaped block and two half-round blocks. No picture of a building stands behind them. Tap a block to pick it up and turn it. A block resting on a curved side rolls. A block on a flat side stays still. No block has a name on it. Then, Practice: Tap the parts. Three pictures come in turn: India Gate, the Qutub Minar and a model street. Tap a part of the picture. For India Gate that is the top, a pillar or the steps. For the street it is a house, a hut or the road. A strip of block cards opens. Tap a card and the block appears beside the part as a see-through ghost. A block that fits glows green and the screen says why. A block that does not fit leaves a gap or sticks out, and the screen says which. Then the child tries another card. India Gate is an arch and the Qutub Minar tapers, so no single block fits them exactly. The screen says so and lets the child stack blocks to come close. The tool's three notice prompts come as thought bubbles after this stage. They are read, not answered. Then, Practice: Hidden shapes. A plain street scene (the model street) holds hidden shapes. The child taps something round, then something with four straight sides. Then comes something with three straight sides and a solid with a point on top. Only objects that truly show the shape are accepted. Last, your maths book's questions, 11 in all, one at a time, in the book's order. Opening, Task: drag blocks onto a build pad to model the gateway with two tall towers and the round hut. Opening, Q1: tap the part words you used (base, pillars or towers, roof). Q2: tap a reason card. Q3: tap a block picture for each part. Q4 and Q5: Compare sets the model beside the real picture, then tap the cards that fit (alike, different). A thought bubble then reads, What would happen if you removed one piece of your model? Would it still look like the building? How could you make it better? Project Work: drag shapes along the road of the model street. Qutub Minar: a child holds a stack of three green boxes and says, I have made something. Look at my Qutub Minar. Q1: tap Yes, A little or No. Q2: tap a shape card and a reason card. Q3: tap a number tile, 1 to 9. A Do you know line reads, The Qutub Minar is a World Heritage site and the tallest building made up of bricks. It has 5 storeys and 379 stairs. Puzzling Shapes, Q1: the red outlines lie over one another. Tap each outline, then tap its name card (circle, square, rectangle, triangle, cylinder). A last line says, You can also model buildings with boxes, bottles, cans and coconut shells.

First, Practice: one line says, Sides, corners and flat or curved parts tell shapes apart. Two real things lie on a desk, a book and a clay water pot. Tap a straight side, a corner or a curved part of either: it lights up softly and its word shows. Nothing is counted. Then, Practice: Three clues. A mystery shape sits behind a cloth. Three clue cards come one at a time. After each clue a tray shows which shapes still fit, and the others turn grey with a reason. The child taps a guess after each clue and may change it. After clue 3 the cloth lifts. Round 1: I have four equal sides. I have four corners. A chessboard has many of my smaller forms. The tray holds a square, a diamond, a long rectangle, a triangle and a circle. A diamond is a leaning shape with four equal sides and no square corner. After clue 2 the square and the diamond both fit, so clue 3 decides. Round 2: I can roll. I have no corner. I have no flat face. The tray holds a ball, a can, a cube and a box. Round 3: I have straight sides. I have three corners. The end of a tent looks like me. The tray holds a triangle, a square, a circle and a slanting four-sided shape. Objects: Bricks (tap the cards that fit: box shape, flat faces, square corners, curved sides). Border Q1 to Q4: the pencil sketches of the book's border are on screen. Flat cards: Card Game (the six cards from the end of the book are on screen). Drag them into three groups, then tap a reason card such as Only straight sides. Cuts: Puzzling Shapes Q2 and Q3. On the dot grid, drag from dot to dot to draw two lines. Q4: drag along the cut lines for shapes A, B and C. Every shape drawn as a solid is a shaded 3D solid.

4. First tower, third layer: 3 × 3 = 9 cubes

9. 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15
10. 4 × 15 = 60
11. 6 + 60 = 66
Answer: From the picture: the first tower has 30 cubes. The second tower has 66 cubes. Both counts include the hidden cubes and assume no gaps.

tool_config.title: Angle Builder
tool_config.learning_objective: Students make angles smaller than, equal to and bigger than a right angle, and find right angles with a paper corner.
tool_config.screen: Frame, the same in every tool: progress dots on top; one stage on screen at a time; Back and Next at the sides and a Hint lamp that gives the four hints one at a time; a wrong try can be tried again and Reset starts the stage over; nothing is timed, scored or counted as a win. Stages that are not questions from your maths book carry a small tag, Practice. Your maths book's questions carry the book's own label, and after each try the screen shows the book's answer, which starts From the picture or Sample answer (open ones end Your answer may differ). First, Practice: one line recalls the idea. Two lines that meet at a point make an angle. The corner of a paper fold is a right angle. A laptop stands open on a table. Drag its lid: the lid and the keyboard are two lines that meet at the hinge, and the angle opens and closes. Then, Practice: Make an angle. Two arms meet at a point on a board. The paper corner lies fixed on the lower arm. It is pale orange paper with a small red square. Drag the other arm. Three challenge cards ask for an angle smaller than, equal to and bigger than a right angle. The screen shows the arm inside the paper corner, on it or outside it. No numbers show. The lower arm is long and the upper arm is short, and both keep their length. The upper arm swings from the lower arm up to a straight line and stops there. No angle is bigger than a straight line. Then, Practice: Check a turned square. A square tile turned on its corner and a slanting four-sided shape lie on the board. Drag the paper corner onto each corner and tap whether it fits. Last, your maths book's questions, 10 in all, one at a time, in the book's order. Example, the house: tap each red mark to count to 7. When Lines Meet, the boat: tap each angle, then tap a number tile. Let Us Do Q1: five pictures (scissors, hanger, hand, seesaw, slide). Tap the places where two lines meet and a red arc appears. Q2: object cards of a classroom (a desk, a door, a clock, a window, a ball and a round plate). Tap the cards that show angles. The ball and the plate show none. Right Angles, make: tap the fold lines to fold the paper in half, then in half again. Then tap the paper to open it. Right Angles, dot grid: eight angles. Tap the ones you think are right angles, then drag the paper corner onto each to check. Right Angles, objects: drag the paper corner onto a corner of a book, a window and one more object. Then tap Right angle or Not a right angle. Let Us Do (right angles) Q1: on the dot grid, drag from a dot to draw a line across. Then draw a line up from the same dot. Check it with the paper corner. Let Us Try Q8: six figures. Drag the paper corner onto each corner, tap the right angles, then tap a number tile for each figure. Then tap the figures that have only right angles.

First, Practice: one line recalls the idea: an acute angle is less than a right angle, and an obtuse angle is more. A paper hand fan lies on a table. Drag its last stick to open it: a little, to a right angle (a small red square), then wide. Each time the screen says smaller than, equal to or bigger than the paper corner. Then, Practice: Sort the angles. Six angles sit in a row: two smaller than a right angle, one right angle and three bigger. They are shown without numbers and all are smaller than a straight line. Three boxes wait: Acute, Right and Obtuse. Drag the paper corner onto an angle to compare. Then drag the angle into a box. The answer shows at once. Last, your maths book's questions, 10 in all, one at a time, in the book's order. Acute and Obtuse Angles, objects (acute): picture cards of classroom objects lie in a row. The cards show a sharp pencil tip, scissors opened a little and a set square's pointed corner. They also show a door opened wide, a laptop lid leaned back and a book's corner. Tap the cards that show an acute angle. Objects (obtuse): tap the cards that show an obtuse angle. Letters: the letters V, A and Z. Tap each place where two strokes meet, then tap Acute, Right or Obtuse. Let Us Do Q1 (acute): on the dot grids, drag from the end of each given line to draw a second line. It must make an acute angle. The paper corner checks each one. Q1 (obtuse): do the same to make an obtuse angle. Q2: four stick figures. Tap an angle, then tap a colour: red for acute, green for right, blue for obtuse. Shapes on a dot grid: drag from dot to dot to draw three- and four-sided shapes. Check the corners with the paper corner, and tap the shapes that have a right angle. Discuss: tap number tiles for how many shapes you made with 1, 2, 3 or all right angles. Four-sided shapes: three four-sided shapes stand beside a rectangle and a square. Drag the paper corner onto their corners, then tap the cards that say how they differ. Let Us Try Q9: fourteen shapes numbered 1 to 14. Tap the shapes that fit each of the four clues. More than one shape may fit a clue. Every answer starts Sample answer, except Q9, which starts From the picture.

tool_config.screen: Frame, the same in every tool: progress dots on top; one stage on screen at a time; Back and Next at the sides and a Hint lamp that gives the four hints one at a time; a wrong try can be tried again and Reset starts the stage over; nothing is timed, scored or counted as a win. First, Practice: one line recalls the idea: a rigid shape keeps its shape when it is pushed. Before any push, the child guesses. Two frames from home are shown and not pushed: a window frame with four sides and a shelf bracket with three sides. Tap the frame you think will keep its shape when pushed. The guess is kept. Then, Practice: Push the frames. A board holds a straw triangle and a straw rectangle joined by clay balls. They lie flat and are pinned to the board along their bottom sides. Drag the top corner of each frame to push it. The rectangle leans into a slanting shape. The triangle does not change. Then tap the frame you think is more rigid. The first guess is shown beside the result. Last, your maths book's questions, 10 in all, one at a time, in the book's order. Shapes with Straws, triangle: drag three straws of different lengths and three clay balls to join a triangle. Push the triangle: push one side, then tap Yes or No. Trace: drag a pencil along the three sides on paper. Angles of a triangle: drag the paper corner onto each corner, then tap Acute, Right or Obtuse for each. Rectangle: drag two long and two short straws and four balls, and push until every corner fits the paper corner. Angles of a rectangle: drag the paper corner onto each corner, then tap a card. Push the rectangle: push one side, then tap Yes or No. The new shape: tap Compare to see before and after. Drag the paper corner onto each corner. Then tap the cards: still right angles, and which kinds. Square: push one side of a square, check the corners, then tap the cards. Compare: tap the cards for how the angles of triangles and rectangles are alike or different.

Tap a card, Yes or No

Reset
tool_config.instruction: Push a corner of each frame. Which one keeps its shape?
feedback: Push the triangle: it does not change. Its three straws cannot change length, so its corners cannot change.
Push the rectangle: it leans over into a slanting shape. The straws keep their length, but the corners turn.
From the picture: before the push the rectangle has 4 right angles. After it, two angles are acute and two are obtuse.
A pushed square does the same: two acute angles and two obtuse angles.
A triangle keeps its shape when it is pushed. It is the most rigid shape.
Sample answer: this triangle has three acute angles. Another triangle can have a right angle or an obtuse angle.
The paper corner decides every angle. Smaller than a right angle is acute. Equal is right. Bigger is obtuse.
A right answer card turns green and says why. A wrong one shakes and shows the corner to check again.

tool_config.title: Shape Identification Quiz
tool_config.learning_objective: Students name each shape in a picture from the chapter, whether a solid, a net, an angle, a circle or a frame.
tool_config.screen: Frame, the same in every tool: progress dots on top; one stage on screen at a time; Back and Next at the sides and a Hint lamp that gives the four hints one at a time; a wrong try can be tried again and Reset starts the stage over; nothing is timed, scored or counted as a win. Stages that are not questions from your maths book carry a small tag, Practice. Your maths book's questions carry the book's own label, and after each try the screen shows the book's answer, which starts From the picture or Sample answer (open ones end Your answer may differ). First, one picture fills the screen, with three name cards under it. The cube tower picture has a number pad and a Check key instead of cards. Each question carries the small tag Practice, and its answer starts From the picture. No picture carries a name, a label or a number that gives the answer away. Every solid is one plain stone-grey tint, shaded and 3D, so colour gives no clue. Then, the child taps the card that names the picture. On the tower picture the child types a number and taps Check. A right answer turns green. The part its reason names lights up, and one reason line shows. A wrong card shakes gently and says what that shape has instead. Then it can be tried again. After the fourth hint, the hint itself greys out one wrong card. After the tenth picture, all ten show again as small tiles. Each tile has its answer line. The ten pictures follow the chapter in this order. The cards stay in the order listed. Picture 1, a solid: a pentagonal pyramid with its hidden edges dashed. Its bottom has five sides. Its five triangle faces meet at one point on top. Question: What is this solid? Cards: Square pyramid, Pentagonal pyramid, Hexagonal prism. Picture 2, a solid: a cylinder standing up. It has two flat round faces and one curved face. Question: What is this solid? Cards: Cylinder, Cone, Sphere. Picture 3, a net: a flat pattern in pale paper with violet dotted fold lines. Three rectangles lie in a row. One triangle joins the top of the middle rectangle. Another joins its bottom. Question: Which solid does this net fold into? Cards: Cube, Square pyramid, Triangular prism. Picture 4, a part of a solid: a cube with one edge lit in amber. Nothing else is marked. Question: What is the lit part? Cards: Edge, Face, Corner. Picture 5, a cube tower of teal cubes with clear edges. The bottom layer is 4 cubes long and 2 wide. A smaller layer of 2 by 2 cubes sits on it. Question: How many cubes are in this tower? The hidden ones count too. Number pad, one or two digits. Picture 6, an angle: a green straw and an orange straw joined by a clay ball. A red arc marks the corner. A folded paper corner lies beside it. The angle is clearly narrower than the paper corner. Question: What kind of angle is this? Cards: Right angle, Obtuse angle, Acute angle. Picture 7, a circle: a plain circle on pale paper with its centre dot showing. One bold line runs across it through the centre dot. Both ends of the line touch the circle. No word is on the picture. Question: What is the bold line? Cards: Radius, Diameter, Centre. Picture 8, a flat shape: a flat purple pentagon, turned a little. No side lies along the bottom. Question: What is this shape? content.text:
1. Think of Isha's straws joined at one end. What do two lines that meet at a point make?
2. They make an angle.
3. Isha opened her straws until they fitted the paper corner exactly. What kind of angle was that?
4. A right angle. The corner of a paper fold is a right angle.
5. Think of the narrow straw corner and the wide one. What are they called?
6. The narrow one is acute: less than a right angle. The wide one is obtuse: more than a right angle.
7. Think of the round paper you folded. Name the centre, the radius and the diameter.
8. The centre is the middle. The radius goes from the centre to the border. The diameter goes across through the centre.
9. Which is longer, the radius or the diameter?
10. The diameter is double the radius.
11. Think of the shape you built from equal straws. How many sides and corners does it have?
12. Five sides and five corners. A shape with five sides is a pentagon.
13. Think of the straw triangle and the straw rectangle. Which one keeps its shape when you push it?
14. The triangle does. A stick across a four-sided frame makes triangles, so the frame stays firm.

visual_key.box_net: a pink paper box opened out flat with dotted fold lines, and a line drawing 'Net of a box' with dotted folds; it folds back into the box (a real paper box, kept pink as in the book; a flat net is never in the colour of a solid)
visual_key.paper_strip_ball: a ball made of curved orange paper strips joined at the top and bottom, with a small green leaf on top (the craft ball of the first Craft task, a paper craft kept orange as in the book; it is not the sphere of the solids)
visual_key.solid_colours: the colour code of the maths solids, one colour per kind of solid in the teaching pictures: prisms blue, pyramids pink, cube teal, cuboid red, sphere coral, cone yellow, cylinder orchid; every solid a shaded 3D solid, with dashed hidden edges where an edge is hidden; in the sorting, matching and riddle stages of the tools every solid is drawn in ONE neutral stone-grey tint (still shaded 3D, so faces and edges show), so that colour never gives the answer; flat shapes in flat colours; a net is never in the colour of its solid; real objects (wooden blocks, bricks, a die, a football, tents, paper boxes) keep their own colours
visual_key.prisms: shaded 3D solids, ALL in the one prism blue (as the book draws them), with dashed hidden edges, labelled Triangular Prism, Square Prism (drawn long, like a box with square ends) and Hexagonal Prism; every other prism of the chapter (a pentagonal prism if one is ever drawn) is this same blue; in the sorting stages the same solids use the one neutral tint instead
visual_key.pyramids: shaded 3D solids, ALL in the one pyramid pink (the book's pink-magenta), with dashed hidden edges, labelled Triangular Pyramid, Square Pyramid and Pentagonal Pyramid; every other pyramid of the chapter is this same pink; in the sorting stages the same solids use the one neutral tint instead
visual_key.sphere: a proper shaded 3D ball with a soft highlight, round from every side, always in the one sphere colour, a coral (a lighter tint of red than the cuboid's deep red, so a sphere and a cuboid on one screen are never alike); never a flat disc; a real ball (a football) keeps its own colours
visual_key.straws_and_clay: thin straws joined at their ends by small round clay balls to make the skeleton of a shape; every straw is its own straight line and every ball its own dot, drawn see-through so no edge hides another and every one can be counted: straws are the edges and balls are the corners (cube and cuboid 12 and 8, triangular pyramid 6 and 4, square pyramid 8 and 5, triangular prism 9 and 6; the model-challenge square pyramid beside the last task is 8 straws and 5 balls). In a SOLID skeleton the straws are in the colour of the solid they make (cube teal, cuboid red, every prism blue, every pyramid pink) and every clay ball is one plain clay colour (a warm grey-brown); in a FLAT straw shape (the triangle, rectangle, square and pentagon of the push tools) the straws stay green, yellow, blue or orange as in the book and the balls red or pink, because a flat shape is not one of the solids
visual_key.die: a standard grey-white die (a real die, so it keeps its own colour and is not the teal cube): opposite faces always add up to 7 (1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4), so two faces that add up to 7 are never in view together; the book's picture shows 5, 1 and 3 on its three visible faces and writes numerals, the same die on every screen
visual_key.colour_cube: one cube with six differently coloured faces, red, orange, green, purple, dark blue and yellow, shown in three views side by side: (top orange, left red, right green), (top purple, left orange, right green), (top red, left dark blue, right yellow); the six face colours are the question's own data, so this cube is NOT teal; the three views must fit one single cube (red opposite purple, yellow opposite orange, dark blue opposite green)
visual_key.border_objects: about twenty pencil sketches round the edge of the Let Us Observe task, in plain pencil outline with grey pencil shading and no colour, so the child's red, blue, smiley and star marks show: 2 dice, 2 erasers, a Rubik's cube, a gift box, 3 balls (one a football), 3 cans or bottles, an ice-cream cone, a party hat, 2 cheese pieces, a pyramid made of small triangles, a double pyramid, a wooden wedge and a cake slice; each is drawn as the book draws it and as itself: every ball a shaded ball, the cone a plain cone with no scoop, a can a cylinder, the wooden wedge and the cake slice triangular prisms, and each cheese piece a pyramid with small holes (never a wedge)
visual_key.sorting_circles: round outlines in dark purple-blue on a pale green panel with green italic labels; two panels have two separate circles, one panel has two overlapping circles with a labelled overlap
visual_key.cube_models: four models of unit cubes in the book's shapes, A, B, C and D (A a block with one step, B a long L-shape, C a stepped pile, D a stepped model of layers 4 by 4, 3 by 3, 2 by 2 and 1 cube); every unit cube is a shaded teal cube, as every cube of the chapter, so the four models differ in shape only (the book prints them red, purple, yellow and blue with teal, pink and green); every unit cube is drawn with its own edges so the cubes can be counted
visual_key.cube_towers: two stacks of unit cubes, every cube a shaded teal cube with clear edges (a light top, a teal left face, a darker right face), the layers told apart by their steps and not by colour: a stepped tower of 4 layers (4 by 4, 3 by 3, 2 by 2 and 1 cube: 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30 cubes, the same shape as model D) and a large plus-shaped tower: a middle column of 6 cubes and four stairs going out from it, each stair with columns of 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 cubes (6 + 4 × 15 = 66 cubes); the figures show only the outside, so the hidden cubes are counted by reading the layers and columns, with solid layers and no gaps (the book's counts of 30 and 66 assume this); the tower of the cube tower video is a different, smaller tower
visual_key.triangular_dot_paper: grey dots in a slanting triangular grid (evenly spaced rows, each row shifted half a step, so any three neighbouring dots make an equal triangle), with one finished cube outline in teal (the cube colour) and two cubes drawn only in dotted lines that run exactly through the dots
visual_key.solid_pictures: shaded 3D pictures, each a true solid in the colour of its kind: beside Q1 a coral sphere with a dashed ring, a pink square pyramid with a hidden corner dashed, a yellow cone, a red cuboid, an orchid cylinder, a teal cube and a small blue triangular prism lying on a rectangle face with its two triangle ends clear (the book's small orange solid, read as a triangular prism); beside Q2 a coral sphere, a yellow cone, a pink triangular pyramid, a teal cube and a red cuboid; a sphere is a shaded ball, a cone has one round flat base and one point, a cylinder has two round flat faces and a curved side; when these solids are the riddle cards of the faces, edges and corners tool they are drawn in the one neutral tint so colour cannot give the answer
visual_key.nets_and_solids: line drawings of nets with dotted fold lines (violet in Q3: a triangle net, a cylinder net, a cuboid net, a triangular prism net; dark green in Q4: four nets) with a solid beside or below each (in a teaching picture in the colour of its kind: cylinder orchid, cube teal, cuboid red, prisms blue, pyramids pink; in the matching stages of the nets tool every solid is drawn in the one neutral tint); a net is flat and is NEVER in the colour of the solid it folds into, so the colour cannot give the match away; every face of a net is its own flat shape joined to the next along a dotted fold line, so the faces can be counted; Nitesh's pieces are pale orange (one pentagon and five triangles) with four solids a to d below; the nets of Q4 are drawn as printed (A and C do not fold)
visual_key.angle_mark: a small red arc at the corner of an angle, or a small red square for a right angle
visual_key.straws_angle: two straws, one green and one orange, meeting at one end to show an angle, with a red arc or red square at the corner
visual_key.yoga_figures: five simple yoga figures with round heads in blue and orange, each with a red arc where two limbs meet
visual_key.house_and_boat: a blue house with a darker blue triangular roof (7 red angle marks) and a boat with a brown hull and a cream sail split by a brown mast into two triangles (10 red angle marks)
visual_key.right_angle_checker: a piece of pale orange paper folded twice so the folded corner is a right angle, marked with a red square
visual_key.dot_grid: rows of black dots on a white page, or on a pale blue, yellow, peach or pink rounded panel
visual_key.angle_figures_grid: eight blue angles drawn on a dot grid in two rows of four; each is two lines meeting at a point
visual_key.angle_pictures: five plain pictures: an open pair of scissors, a clothes hanger, a hand making a V sign, a seesaw and a slide; in each the two arms that meet are drawn clearly
visual_key.angle_letters: the capital letters V, A and Z in large plain strokes, one angle of each marked in red
visual_key.stick_figures: four simple stick people with round faces, whose arms and legs meet at angles
visual_key.rigid_shapes: straw shapes joined by red or pink clay balls: a triangle (made by a girl in a pink top on a purple rug), a rectangle of blue straws with a second drawing of it pushed over into a slanted shape, a square, and a pentagon of five equal blue straws with grey-pink clay balls; each clay ball is a joint that lets a shape turn, so a push tilts a four-sided or five-sided shape but never a triangle
visual_key.four_sided_shapes: three flat 4-sided shapes: a green shape with a slanted side, a pink slanting shape and an orange diamond (in this chapter a diamond always means one thing: a leaning shape with four equal sides and no right angle; a square turned on its corner is called a square turned on its corner)
visual_key.equal_straws_circle: many straws in different colours, all the same length, laid like spokes round a central clay ball so that their ends make a circle; and the same straws with unequal lengths, whose ends do not make a circle
visual_key.circle_paper: a round sheet of orange-brown paper with dashed fold lines through the middle (creases); a red circle with the labels Diameter and Radius on a half and a quarter fold
visual_key.compass_design: a yellow circle (Step 1), overlapping dotted circles (Step 2), then a six-petal flower made of overlapping circles in blue, green, red and yellow (Step 3)
visual_key.compass: a school compass: two arms joined at the top, a sharp metal point on one arm and a pencil on the other; the point stays fixed on the centre and the pencil draws the circle
visual_key.carpet_design: a brown carpet with a fringe, a paisley border and an orange circle in the middle holding green and yellow petals around a small blue centre
visual_key.wheels: four wheels labelled A to D: a grey car wheel with four oval holes, a large brown wooden spoked wheel, a bicycle wheel with blue spokes and a thin black tyre, and a small dark tyre with a silver rim; each seen straight on so it is a true circle with its centre showing, in the printed sizes (B the largest, then C, then A, and D the smallest)
visual_key.hidden_shapes: red outlines drawn over one another: a circle, a cylinder, one upright square, one tilted rectangle (about 2.2 times as long as wide) and two triangles (six shapes); all one red on purpose, so they hide one another; the cylinder here is a line drawing in that red, not the orchid solid
visual_key.dissection_shapes: flat coloured shapes: an orange long hexagon, a green square and a pink triangle on the left, and the smaller pieces they are cut into on the right
visual_key.shape_cards: six flat cut-out cards from the end of the book: an orange square, a green oval, a brown quarter circle, a light-green semicircle, a blue triangle and a pink circle
visual_key.spider_webs: purple threads on white: Squiggly's web is a long shape with 12 walls numbered 1 to 12 in dark red and point A at the bottom tip (the numbers follow one walk from A round to A); Wiggly's web is a set of rectangles with a short bar at the top, point A at the bar's upper right end and point B at the bottom of the second line from the left; these are the figures of the strong structure tool, and the two webs story draws two simple webs of its own instead
visual_key.matchsticks: a thin wooden stick with a red head at one end, all the same length, every stick drawn whole so the sticks can be counted: Q2 five loose sticks and a dashed drawing box; Q3 nine sticks as three small triangles in a row that touch at the base corners (the book draws small gaps; here the corners touch, because only then can the puzzle be solved); Q4 thirteen sticks making six small triangles (a big triangle of side 2 with one small triangle on its upper left side and one on its lower right side); all corners meet on one triangular grid
visual_key.angle_shapes: flat coloured 2D shapes in Q6: a blue square, a red triangle, a green slanting 4-sided shape, a purple right triangle, a purple pentagon, a thin green triangle and a red rectangle
visual_key.right_angle_figures: six flat coloured figures in Q8 in a row: a blue rectangle, a green slanting 4-sided shape, a purple triangle, an orange 4-sided shape wider at the top, a purple slanting 4-sided shape and a red tilted rectangle (a little longer than wide, as the book draws it: a rectangle, not a square); every corner drawn true
visual_key.shape_gallery: fourteen flat coloured shapes numbered 1 to 14 in Q9 in three rows, mostly 4-sided (squares, rectangles and slanting shapes) with one dart-shaped number 1; every corner drawn true so right, acute and obtuse angles can be told apart
visual_key.prism_tent: a real camping tent with two matching triangle ends and three rectangle faces (two slanting sides and the floor), straight edges, as a clean shaded illustration standing on grass; one plain tent colour, the same as the pyramid tent, so colour is no clue (not the prism blue); the face shapes are marked with light outlines, never counted or named
visual_key.pyramid_tent: a real tent with a square floor and four triangle faces that meet at one point at the top, straight edges, as a clean shaded illustration standing on grass beside the prism tent; the same plain tent colour as the prism tent (not the pyramid pink); the face shapes are marked with light outlines, one marking for triangles on both tents, never counted or named

story.thread: Diksha visits Delhi with her father, sees its old and new monuments and tries to build a model of India Gate from her wooden blocks; the children and the spiders Squiggly and Wiggly then meet solid shapes, nets, angles, circles and shape puzzles.
story.setting: a floor mat where Diksha builds with wooden blocks after her summer trip to Delhi (India Gate, Qutub Minar and other monuments); a classroom and craft table with straws, clay, paper, matchsticks and a compass; two spider webs
